svg.text: Four formulas, and the sense-check that catches the decimal point
Tablets and liquids
WANT / HAVE x VOLUME
What you want, over what the stock is,
times the volume that stock comes in.
Both must be in the SAME unit before you divide.
Drops per minute
VOLUME x DROP FACTOR / MINUTES
Millilitres times the drops per mL that the
giving set delivers, over the total minutes.
Hours must become minutes first. Multiply by 60.
Millilitres per hour
TOTAL VOLUME / HOURS
The simplest one, and the one pumps use.
No drop factor is involved at all.
A pump is set in mL/h; a gravity set is counted in drops.
Weight-based dose
DOSE PER KG x WEIGHT
Work out the total dose FIRST, then apply
the want-over-have step to find the volume.
Two steps. Do not try to do them in one line.
The unit ladder — most errors are a factor of 1,000
1 g = 1,000 mg 1 mg = 1,000 microgram 1 L = 1,000 mL
Going DOWN the ladder to a smaller unit, the number gets BIGGER — multiply.
Going UP to a larger unit, the number gets SMALLER — divide.
Never write a bare decimal point. Write 0.5 mg, never .5 mg — the dot is lost and the dose becomes tenfold.
The sense-check, every single time
Ask: is this a believable number for a real patient?
More than 2 tablets, or more than 2 ampoules, for one dose — stop and recheck.
A drip rate under 5 or over 100 drops a minute — stop and recheck.
An answer that is exactly 10 or 100 times out is the commonest error there is. The check is what catches it.
